content.title: How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO
content.full_text: Image Credits: CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP / Getty Images Venture How Notable Capital, GIC, and Baillie Gifford bet big on Anthropic before its IPO Marina Temkin 5:25 PM PST · November 22, 2026 When Notable Capital poured roughly 10% of the U.S. portion of its $1 billion-plus fund into Anthropic’s Series E, many limited partners were perplexed by the massive bet. Claude’s maker was still trailing its biggest rival, OpenAI, and DeepSeek had released its R1 model just weeks earlier, threatening to overtake closed-source competitors. Moreover, at $61.5 billion, Anthropic’s valuation was by far the highest that the predominantly early-stage venture firm had invested at in its 25-year history. But investors at Notable, formerly known as GGV Capital before its 2024 split from its China operations, were confident in Anthropic’s future. A team that included managing partners Hans Tung and Glenn Solomon and principal Dan Cahana crunched the numbers and found that developers were increasingly favoring Claude over ChatGPT, using Claude 70% of the time, a reversal from the previous year. “We just knew that for AI, the developer is at the center because they’re the early adopters,” Tung, a co-founder of the firm, told TechCrunch. Having navigated the complexities of U.S.-China relations firsthand, Notable was also convinced that “mission-critical” work would always require U.S.-based, closed-source models, Tung said. Less than two years later, Notable’s LPs are no longer questioning the outsized investment. On Wednesday, Anthropic raised $81.3 billion in the largest IPO in history, reaching a fully diluted valuation of about $1.5 trillion before its shares began trading the next day, a paper return of roughly 15 times. Notable is, of course, not the only firm sitting on a massive paper windfall from Anthropic. Even traditional late-stage investors, who rarely see venture-scale multiples, are set for a big win. Singaporean sovereign wealth fund GIC had been researching Anthropic throughout 2024, but it didn’t make its first investment until after Chris Emanuel, head of the fund’s tech investments, met with Anthropic CFO Krishna Rao at Che Fico, an Italian restaurant in San Francisco, in early 2025. Rao helped pique Emanuel’s interest in the company by showing that model improvements were driving rising enterprise adoption. GIC then made its first investment in Anthropic’s Series F, a round announced in September 2025 at a $183 billion valuation. “Claude Code was just released then,” Emanuel told TechCrunch. “It was very early, but even then, we could see signs that it was really popular with developers.” GIC’s conviction in the AI lab was so high that the fund later led Anthropic’s Series G alongside Coatue at a $380 billion valuation, and returned as one of the co-leads for the pre-IPO round at $965 billion. Across the three rounds, GIC invested more than $4.5 billion in Anthropic, amassing a stake equal to about 1% of the company after its IPO, according to a person familiar with GIC’s financials. Lilian Li, who leads U.S. growth investments at Baillie Gifford, began studying Anthropic and speaking with its team nearly two years before first investing in the company’s Series F. Baillie Gifford invested in the Claude maker once it became clear that the company was “executing consistently” on its vision while generating strong revenue and “compelling gross margins,” Li told TechCrunch. After Baillie Gifford’s initial investment, Anthropic continued to deliver on its promises, expanding into industries such as legal services and life sciences, as well as broader applications like Cowork and cybersecurity, Li said. “It’s actually quite incredible how consistent they have been with how quickly everything’s been changing,” she added. Baillie Gifford went on to invest a total of $1.5 billion across three funding rounds, a bet that has generated substantial paper gains for the investment manager, as well as for dozens of other backers who invested at what once seemed like astronomical valuations. content.title: OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development
content.full_text: Image Credits: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto / Getty Images AI OpenAI’s chief scientist has thoughts on how to limit AI development Anthony Ha 1:14 PM PST · November 22, 2026 A new blog post from OpenAI’s chief scientist Jakub Pachocki discusses potential limits on AI development, with a focus on a measurement called perplexity. Slowing AI development became a particularly hot topic after a former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher said the companies were “gambling with our lives,” and even Anthropic’s IPO filing suggested that the technology could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to society.” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei then published a plan to “pace the frontier,” seemingly endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. Among other things, Amodei called for companies to agree to “common safety standards as well as limits on the rate of unchecked AI progress.” But to establish a speed limit on AI development, you need to agree on how you measure speed. Pachocki’s post — described by Altman as “the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while” — suggests perplexity (not to be confused with the company of the same name ) could be that measurement. In Pachochki’s argument, benchmarks that focus on AI’s “downstream capabilities” have quickly become outdated as the technology advances. But perplexity — which “measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions” — has remained “informative.” Pachochki’s post includes a chart of how the perplexity of OpenAI’s models has fallen since GPT 3.5. “GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models,” he wrote. “Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics.” So in his view, perplexity could provide the basis for “a shared benchmark for general intelligence,” which AI companies could then use to establish “common limits.” With perplexity serving as a standard measurement for AI progress, the companies would commit not to go past a certain threshold “until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone.” Topics AI , OpenAI , sam altman When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . content.title: Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash
content.full_text: Image Credits: Ethan Cairns/Bloomberg / Getty Images AI Why data centers are at the center of the Big Tech backlash Anthony Ha 10:08 AM PST · November 22, 2026 In his new book “Hyperscale,” journalist Paris Marx investigates the impact of data centers and generative AI, taking readers inside the data centers themselves and explaining how computing infrastructure that goes back decades recently became a political landmine. The book is well-timed, to put it mildly, as data center backlash seems to have been one of the motivators for the massive blue wave seen in the recent midterm elections . And those debates are likely to continue as Democrats wield more governmental power . In an interview with TechCrunch, Marx described the data center buildout as “fundamentally unsustainable” and “completely out of line with a livable planet,” while also arguing that these facilities make for an obvious target amidst broader anger at the tech industry. After all, if a data center is being built in your community, “it’s very physical, it’s very material.” “It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on,“ Marx said. “You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise.” He also suggested that data center opposition is only the most visible piece of a wider movement targeting “the physical manifestations of the tech industry, […] whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out.” During our conversation (which I’ve edited for length and clarity), Marx and I discussed data centers’ environmental impact, how tech companies are responding to community resistance, and what it’s actually like inside a data center. I liked your description of trying to get access to the inside of a “hyperscale” data center and then eventually taking a tour [of one]. Could you talk a little bit more about what that experience was like? How did you get in? What surprised you when you actually got in? Getting inside of a hyperscale data center was not the easiest task in the world. I spoke to some researchers who have been doing research on data centers for a number of years longer than I had, and they told me that before the generative AI moment, and before all the attention that has been put on data centers recently, that it was quite a bit easier to do so. I sent emails to a number of companies asking if I could get inside, often didn’t get a response, other times got a no. I ended up, after visiting the outsides of some data centers in places like northern Virginia and Ireland and spots like that, I actually went down to New Zealand to go inside of a data center itself.  And the thing that struck me most was the level of security. Obviously, you would expect that this is an infrastructure that is really securitized, because the data inside needs to be kept safe, obviously [they] have these big fences and all the security cameras around the data centers. But to go inside, I had to send my passport in advance. Then when I got there, they had to check the passport, and then as we were going through the data center itself, every single door in the data center was locked unless you had a key card to unlock it. Then, when you get inside of the server room itself, where all this computer hardware is stored in tall racks that look like cabinets — you can imagine, in your mind, that this would be kind of a sinister location, with some eerie lighting or something like that. But in truth, it’s just quite utilitarian. It’s a warm room with some air conditioning blasting into the servers from vents that are nearby. It was really loud as well, because you have all these fans running from all these servers, it was really kind of piercing. To be inside of this room, if you were going to be in there for a while, you’d probably want earplugs or something like that. Before I read your book, I thought of data centers as something that’s important, but a little bit boring. How did you decide they were interesting and rich enough to sustain an entire book? I felt the same. I was aware that data centers had been out there, but it was not something that I was paying particularly close attention to. But then there were a number of stories that of tipped me off to the fact that there might be more here, and that it was worth looking deeper into what was going on — the first being hearing about the water pressures created by data centers in Chile around the capital of Santiago , where companies like Google and Microsoft were building data centers, and communities were concerned about their access to water and started organizing around that. And then hearing about how much electricity data centers were consuming in Ireland, to the point that now they consume more than 20% of the country’s electricity , and that was obviously pushing up power prices. It was putting pressures on the grid, such that the grid operator actually put a moratorium in place for grid connections for data centers around the Dublin area, back in 2022. This was even before the generative AI moment that caused a surge in construction of data centers. And then the other one was in The Dalles, Oregon, where Google had actually built its first company-owned data centers about 20 years back. In that case, its water deal was coming up for renewal. It wanted to build more data centers there, so it needed more water. And when the residents started asking, “How much water is Google actually using?” a journalist at The Oregonian went to the city and essentially asked, “Hey, how much water is Google using? Our readers would like to know this,” he was hit with a lawsuit instead of being given that information. Because Google did not want it to be public. And then, of course, when it did come out about a year later, Google revealed that it was using 29% of the city’s water, which seemed quite significant. That was around when ChatGPT was being released and generative AI was starting to take off. It felt like, okay, there are these pockets of places where a lot of data centers have already been constructed, where they are putting pressures on the communities that are causing people to respond, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities. It was a good time to really start to dig in and pay attention. You don’t just talk about the data centers’ environmental impact, but also, they [become] your way in to talk about this broader tech moment. They represent to you — particularly the hyperscale data centers — represent to you how these tech companies are doing business now. Absolutely. The hyperscale data centers and just the scale of the construction — whether it’s the the size of the actual facilities themselves or the number that these companies are trying to build out, just feels fundamentally unsustainable. They’re just demanding too much from the communities where they’re being located, whether that’s because of electricity or because of water use or what have you, or just the fact that they’re building out so many, that when you think about the cumulative impact and you look at the demand for water, but particularly for energy from fossil fuels, that means that it’s just completely out of line with a livable planet and an amount of computation that feels like it makes any degree of sense for us to have constructed. I think it really goes back to the hubris of the tech industry and of these major tech companies and the tech billionaires that run them, and the fact that they have these particular visions of the future that are based on fantasies , but also on expanding their own power and influence over the world, and they don’t seem to mind that everyone else then has to pay the cost that comes with their ambitions and what they are seeking to do. And I feel like it’s become particularly egregious with generative AI and the data centers to power them, where many of the benefits that were supposed to come of generative AI do not appear to have materialized — whether those are the economic benefits, the productivity benefits, but also the the benefits of delivery of services like healthcare and education to the public, as we heard Sam Altman saying a lot in the in the early days of ChatGPT. Paired with that, there has been this massive environmental cost […] but there’s also this massive and growing social cost, when you think about the mental health impacts of chatbot dependence, of all the false information that pervades social media platforms now, of the deepfake crisis, and I could go on and on and on. It’s not surprising that there has been backlash. But I have been surprised at how widespread it’s been, and also how bipartisan — you talk about Ron DeSantis and Bernie Sanders both being opposed to data centers. Why do you think it’s become such a unifying issue? Because it’s not an abstract issue, right? I think even when we think about generative AI or social media or something like that, [it] can feel abstract. It’s a service that you access from your phone or from your computer. It’s not something that is tangible in the world. But when a data center is coming to set up shop in your community, it’s very physical, it’s very material. It doesn’t matter what side of the political spectrum that you’re on. You are going to feel the effects of that in your quality of life, in your power bill, potentially in your access to water, potentially in what you hear around your community, if these air conditioning units on the roofs of data centers are making a lot of noise. I think that there was already a pre-existing frustration with the tech industry that came from the quality of the products, the effects that they’re having on our society and our lives. For some people, [they have] frustration with the way that the tech industry has been collaborating with the Trump administration and with right-wing political groups in different parts of the world. But then you add on top of that the actual effects that come of having one of these infrastructures be planned or located in your community, and that anger gets kind of directed into that physical manifestation of this thing that you have an issue with. Obviously, the data centers are at the forefront of this, and it’s what we pay the most attention to. But we also see this increasingly with other aspects of the tech industry, whether it’s the opposition to Flock cameras rolling out across the United States, or the smart glasses that Meta is trying to put on people’s faces, or even the self-driving cars that Waymo is rolling out. There’s a lot of frustration with the physical manifestations of the tech industry, because that is something that can really be felt more directly, but can also be challenged more directly. You can delete an app on your phone, but what difference does that really make to the company? It doesn’t often seem like very much. The tech companies have reacted to this backlash in a few different ways. One is that Microsoft, Amazon, and  OpenAI have all talked about [their commitment] that they’re not going to use NDAs anymore in their negotiations with local governments. How big a difference do you think that will make? Not a huge difference. I do think it’s going to be good that it will be easier for people to access information on these projects that are being located in their communities. But part of the reason why we’re seeing these shifts is exactly in response to that opposition. We’re seeing the tech companies propose to pay for more of the electricity infrastructure that will be required for their data centers to reduce the pressure on ratepayers, because people are angry about that. They’re promising to use different water-based cooling systems in their data centers, to say that they’re able to use less electricity. When we look at the NDAs and the decision or the announcement that they’re not going to use those anymore, I think it’s also because it’s working against them. People know what a data center is now, and if people find out that a data center is coming to town and they have questions and they’re not getting answers, that’s only going to further fuel the opposition to those data centers. So, it’s not really a surprise to see [the tech companies] do this, and it’s a way that they can get a positive PR thing by saying, “We’re not going to use these NDAs that are working against us anyway. “ One of the other ways they’ve responded is by saying that there’s a lot of misinformation about the environmental harms, or that they’re being overstated, or that they can mitigate them with renewable technology. How valid do you think those arguments are? I think that the industry recognizes that there is a lot of concern and they’re trying to basically move into the discussion with narratives of their own to have people question whether data centers are really a problem or not. I feel like we don’t see the industry doing as much on the energy side anymore, particularly on the fossil fuel side, because they realize that they have kind of lost that argument. If you look back a year and a half, two years ago, they were talking a lot about renewables , about nuclear energy, you don’t hear so much of that discourse anymore. They have pivoted, instead, to focus on the water question, where I think that they feel that they can use more abstract national figures in order to confuse the public about what’s going on. They can say, “If you look nationally, agriculture and golf courses also use a lot of water. So you don’t need to be worried about a data center coming to tow,n because they don’t use as much, in aggregate.” But the issue with data center water use is not a national issue. It’s a local issue. There are unquestionably going to be communities where they seek to locate data centers that are going to have plenty of water and that are not going to be concerned about a data center coming to town. But they’re also locating [data centers] in a lot of communities that are experiencing high degrees of water stress, which means that they don’t have the water to really provide to these infrastructures. We have also seen them pivoting to move away from the evaporative cooling systems, the ones that require a lot of water — because you need to take in a certain amount of water as it gets too hot, it evaporates away, and so you can see why you need a consistent flow of water into the data center for that type of cooling system —  to a closed loop system, where you basically have a certain amount of water, it stays within the data center, you keep cooling it down by using electricity to do that, and so you clearly don’t need as much water. That is their new way to say, “Hey, don’t worry about the water use. We’re going to switch to this other system.” But the issue there, of course, is that it does require more electricity in order to keep that water cooled down, and that is often not part of what they talk about or discuss when they are proposing that as an alternative. Then the other thing is that it’s not just water that is in those pipes or tubes going through the data center. There’s also a lot of coolant in there, a lot of chemicals, and communities where these projects are being located with closed loop cooling systems are becoming increasingly concerned about those coolants leaking out into their water supply and what that is going to mean. In the book, you say repeatedly that you’re not against technology itself or even data centers in general, but [against] this hyperscale approach. The book is called “Hyperscale.” The last chapter is called “Human Scale.” Why do you see scale as such an important part of the problem? Because scale is what creates the pressures, whether those are the pressures on the communities or you know the pressures on our wider electricity system and whatnot. I don’t think that the inherent problem is data centers, because we have had data centers for a long time, and sure, there have been occasional concerns about specific projects, but data centers as a whole have not been an issue that the public has felt merited this degree of attention. So that is why I feel the hyperscale data center, and particularly the acceleration that we’ve seen in the expansion of the size of these hyperscale data centers, but also the number of data centers that these companies are building out, is notable in this moment. Linked to that is not just the scale of the demand created by these hyperscale data centers, but also, what they are supposed to be powering? That is where the other disconnect lies. They’re demanding a lot, but if we were actually getting something good for it, this might be justified. I think that for a lot of people, and I feel like we see this reflected in polling, they’re not actually seeing the benefits from generative AI. So then the question becomes: “Okay, we’re expending all of these resources, we’re pushing up emissions such that climate change is going to be accelerated just to build out all these data centers to meet the ambitions of generative AI that the tech companies have, but then we’re not actually getting much benefit out of that technology. So what are we actually doing here?” One other thing that really struck a chord with me was your description about how tech executives often talk about the future as if there’s [just one] inevitable future. The only thing that’s in question is how quickly we arrive there [and] who’s going to make the most money off of it. This is so important for me, because I do feel like how we think about the future then shapes decisions that we make. The tech billionaires, they see the future in a certain way […] and I think that they have been very successful in getting us to buy into their vision of the future for the past several decades. But that does not mean that that is the only way that the future has to be. We can imagine a very different kind of future, and that would mean that we place our resources in different places and actually develop technology in a different way, toward different outcomes, with different incentives driving that work. There are interesting conversations happening in different parts of the world right now around things like digital sovereignty, getting off of these technologies from the U.S. tech companies. But in some cases, those conversations are quickly captured by industry in those different parts of the world to say, “Okay, we want to get off U.S. technology, but let’s have our local companies do effectively the same thing, and just let them do the same exploitative practices and make the money that the U.S. tech companies would be making.” And I don’t think that that is the right way forward. I also think that there is a role for public sector development of technology in a way that we’ve eschewed or even looked at skeptically for the past number of decades, because the idea was that technology had to be left to the private sector. What we’re starting to see in Europe is a bit more funding of public technology, in order to develop the services that government itself depends on, and I think that that is a good first step. But especially when we’re looking at the Microsoft outage that happened just recently, and we’re looking at Google threatening schools with their access to Google search if they don’t accept Google AI tool, I think that there’s a real moment right now to put resources into developing something different, that doesn’t come from these major tech companies, and that hopefully can have much more public benefit than what these companies now provide us. content.title: A Beginner's Guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth
content.full_text: A beginner's guide to Local AI with Inkling, Qwen, and Unsloth We have AI at home! Set up your own free personal ChatGPT on your PC with Unsloth and Inkling or Qwen. It's private, and the whole house can use it. By Jerry James · Nov 22, 2026 With the launch of open-weight models like Qwen, cloud-based LLM providers seem like they're more of infrastructure or appliance businesses when it comes to most routine tasks that an AI model can handle. OpenAI and Anthropic have displayed a pattern of dropping model quality in the 'latest' version and controlling exactly what you're allowed to run on their models. Add to this ballooning costs and privacy concerns, and we get a pretty good case for moving away from this 'convenient' cloud experience. That's basically where I was too. I wanted to offload certain token-heavy research, data collection, or coding tasks to an AI model without staring at usage limits all day. So, as any reasonable human being would do, I decided to set up my own local AI : a Claude and ChatGPT replacement that runs at home on my own hardware. Since this was my first attempt, my primary focus was keeping it simple and hosting it on Windows. If you're a beginner, you can follow along to get one going on your home network too. Once you have the hardware sorted, it takes about 10-15 minutes (excluding download times). The short version Install Unsloth Desktop, download a quantized AI model that fits your GPU's VRAM, set your context size, and turn on LAN access so everyone at home can use it. What Do You Need to Run a Local AI at Home? Not much (other than the hardware). Here's a short list: A Windows PC with a graphics card (GPU). The more video memory (VRAM) it has, the bigger the model it can run. I'm using an RTX 5090 with 32GB VRAM for this setup. Unsloth Desktop. A free app that 'serves' the AI model to you through a chat interface. Get it from Unsloth . An AI model sized to fit your GPU. We'll pick one in the next section. That's it. No terminal commands, Python environments, or subscriptions required. Which AI Model Can Your GPU Run? It depends on how much VRAM your graphics card has. As a rough guide, 8-12GB of VRAM handles smaller 9B-12B models, while 32GB comfortably runs 27B-35B models with plenty of room for long conversations. On consumer-grade hardware, we'll need smaller models. The full-size Qwen model sits at around 56GB and won't really fit on a consumer graphics card unless you're running a Mac with unified memory. That's where quantization comes in. What Is Quantization? Quantization shrinks a model by compressing weights and moving to a lower precision. You basically trade some accuracy for a model that actually fits on your GPU and runs faster. The same photo stored at 8, 4 and 2 bits per pixel. A model's weights lose detail the same way going from Q8 to Q4 to Q2. If you're wondering whether this tradeoff is worth it, well, it depends. You'll find that certain types of workloads don't really care and give similar outputs, while others may be nearly unusable. Which Model Should You Run for Your VRAM? For this guide, we'll be going with Qwen3.8-27B with 4-bit quantization on my system with an RTX 5090. Going up a tier is an option thanks to its 32GB of VRAM, but I wanted to allow for a larger context window (how much of the conversation the model can keep in mind at once) rather than cramming in the largest model that fits. Qwen3.8-27B at each precision with a 128K context, from our VRAM calculator . At 4-bit, the model and the context fit a 32 GB card with room to spare. If you want to run a model of this caliber with excellent performance, a hilariously overpriced RTX 5090 (remember when $1,999 felt too high?) is unfortunately still not a terrible 'deal' these days. The other option is way more expensive enterprise-grade GPUs . If you're on a GPU with less VRAM, you can still get something very usable going right away. The table below gives you a rough idea of where you can start. They keep a decent speed on a smaller card with the rest held in system RAM, which is why a 35B model sits in the 16 GB row. On an RTX 5060 Ti 16GB, our calculator puts Qwen3.6-35B at about 47 tokens per second this way. Feel free to experiment with several models until you find one that fits your needs. You can also use GPUPartner's VRAM Calculator to get an estimate. Can You Run Inkling 2 on an RTX 5090? Inkling 2 Mini, yes. Inkling 2 Small, no. Inkling 2 Mini is the newest model in this size class. Thinking Machines Lab released it on November 17, 2026: 26.4B parameters, Apache 2.0, vision support and a 1M-token context. Unsloth's recommended file, UD-Q4_K_XL, is 17.6 GB. That is within 0.1 GB of the Qwen3.8-27B file in this guide, so it sits on a 32GB card the same way and leaves about 14GB for context. Nothing else in this guide changes. Update Unsloth Desktop first, because Inkling 2 needs a recent build, then search for Inkling 2 Mini in the same drop-down in Step 2. They count RAM and VRAM together and cover the model alone, so a long context needs more. Inkling 2 Mini is a mixture-of-experts model with 5.4B parameters active, so the 4-bit file also runs on a 16 GB card with the remainder in system RAM, a little slower. Inkling 2 Small is small in name only. It is a 594B model, and the smallest file Unsloth publishes is 171.7 GB. That is unified-memory territory: a 256GB Mac Studio or a DGX Station , not a graphics card. Can You Run a Local AI on a Mac? Yes. You'll find good alternatives in Apple's Mac lineup thanks to its unified memory . Macs are pretty good at running larger models, even if they don't offer the best performance. Just make sure you grab the MLX flavor that is custom-built for Apple Silicon. The same trade applies to unified-memory PCs like the MSI PRO MAX EDGE AI+ 11M and NVIDIA's DGX Spark . How Do You Set Up a Local AI with Unsloth Desktop? It takes three steps: install Unsloth Desktop, download your model, and set the context size. I'll go over these steps in more detail below so you can follow along. Step 1: Install Unsloth Desktop First, we'll need a solution that 'serves' the AI model to you. My pursuit of simplicity narrowed my choices down to LM Studio or Unsloth Desktop. Both abstract away a ton of terminal commands and handle Python environments and dependencies behind a nice, simple UI, which makes them excellent picks for a first home setup. I landed on Unsloth Desktop mostly because, well, I liked the name better. Also, it didn't try to push the very thing I was trying to escape when I opened its website: a subscription. The community seems to like it overall too, so that's another point in its favor. Once you've clicked through the installer and launched Unsloth, you'll see a window like this one. Unsloth Desktop on first launch, before any model is loaded. Step 2: Download a Quantized Model On the top left of this main window, you can pick the model that you want to use from the drop down. We'll be using Qwen3.8-27B. The model picker. Qwen3.8-27B is first on the Recommended list. You should see a submenu like the one below when you click on a model. I'll be using Unsloth's UD-Q4_K_XL version. The M and S versions are smaller, but the XL version behaves much closer to the full-size model without filling up our VRAM, so it seemed like a good pick for my GPU. Every quantization of Qwen3.8-27B with its download size. The gear next to the downloaded one holds the context setting. Step 3: Set the Context Size Once the download completes, you should see a gear icon to the right of the model as shown in the screenshot above. Here, you can set your context size manually or leave it on Auto if you aren't sure how much you need. I'll be setting mine to 128K (unquantized) and might reassess after I've run the model through a few of my routine tasks for a few weeks. Again, you can use this VRAM calculator to help you with these numbers for your specific GPU . At this point, our first local AI is up and running, and you can start chatting with it right inside Unsloth. Remember, your mileage may vary depending on your setup. How Do You Share a Local AI Across Your Home Network? Short answer: Unsloth Desktop has LAN sharing built in. Set a Remote password, start LAN access, and share the address it gives you with anyone on your home network. Once Unsloth Desktop is set up with a model, you might want to give family members or friends access too. For now, we'll only serve it over our local network, so my family can use it without needing physical access to this PC. Head into Unsloth Desktop settings (gear icon on bottom left), and look for the 'Remote & LAN' tab. Settings, Remote & LAN. LAN access is the second card. The Remote access card above it is for a later part. Most of this section will be greyed out until you set a Remote password. Once you've set a password, you'll see a 'Start' button for LAN access. Click that and you should see an address that anyone on your home network can open in a browser to use a local AI model within a chat interface. They'll sign in as 'unsloth' with the Remote password you set. Just keep in mind that the PC needs to stay on with Unsloth running for anyone to reach it. Can You Access Your Local AI Across the Internet? Soon™ Not with this setup alone. Everything so far is limited to your local home network. If you just need a chat interface like ChatGPT, Gemini, etc. to work within your home network, you're basically done at this point! You and anyone on your network can start talking to an AI model hosted on your machine right away. In the next parts, we'll cover performance, tunneling, as well as setting up an agent that runs locally and uses only the web tools you allow it to use. This will let you automate more complex tasks like coding, research, and so much more without being tied to a subscription or usage limits and censorship. As always, my focus remains simplicity that allows my family to use it without too much guidance or help. PS. If you have any recommendations for agentic harnesses or even models to try, feel free to let me know and I'll give them a go! content.title: AI is becoming a disaster for the climate
content.full_text: AI is becoming a disaster for the climate Two new studies reveal the exploding carbon emissions of the AI industry, while Silicon Valley pushes to kill communities’ means of protesting data centers and the impacts on human health mount. Brian Merchant Nov 22, 2026 Listen 157 23 67 Anthropic’s initial public offering netted the company over $81 billion on the first day of trading, making it one of, if not the , largest IPOs in history. The leading AI company, just five years old, now officially boasts a net worth in the neighborhood of $1.3-$1.7 trillion, depending on how you do your accounting. I think this is a good time, as such, to point out that, per a recent report , Anthropic also “has one of the worst recent records on fossil fuels, with analysis showing its upcoming data center projects could emit nearly 20 megatons of CO2-e a year.” Despite effectively positioning itself as a uniquely ethical AI company, Anthropic has been doubling down on fossil fuels to power its technology, both by turning to particularly polluting data centers, like xAI’s infamous Colossus plant in Memphis, for its compute needs, and embracing natural gas to power its own rapidly expanding array of in-house data centers. Anthropic, of course, is not alone. Despite all the whipsawing AI news of late—Jensen Huang’s ouster at Nvidia and failed comeback bid , the digital infrastructurapocalpyse of the last week, and the IPO, for starters—I was glad to see another study, on the climate impacts of the AI buildout, get some serious headlines. Even if those headlines were all of the ‘rather alarming’ variety, like the New York Times’, which went “Carbon Emissions of Biggest U.S. Data Centers Already Rival Entire Countries, Study Reveals.” I was less glad to see BAAJA, a permitting reform bill designed to overturn key environmental protections in the name of making it easier for developers to build energy infrastructure and data centers, pass the Senate. We’ll get into all this, and a bit more, including a cameo from a very special guest who might help prove that data center skepticism runs in the family, in today’s edition. As always, this work is made possible by my magnificent paid subscribers—thank you, thank you—who chip in a few bucks a month so I can keep the lights on. If you’re able, and you find value in this work, please consider upgrading, too. Okay! Onwards. Subscribe First, let’s get to that Harvard University study that made waves right before the Anthropic IPO. The report examined the CO2 emissions of over 400 of the United States’ largest data centers. It found that more than half of the power used to run them, 54%, was generated by fossil fuels, and thus, combined, they emitted as much carbon pollution as a mid-sized nation. Here’s the New York Times: The largest data centers in the United States are responsible for an estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions annually — almost as much as entire countries like Bolivia or Denmark — according to new research. The study , published Monday in the journal Nature Sustainability, delivers the first peer-reviewed estimates of carbon dioxide emissions from the country’s biggest data centers since the start of the artificial intelligence boom. Its authors, a team led by researchers from Harvard University, examined the electricity consumption and carbon emissions of 403 data centers from May 2024 to April 2025. All told, those data centers used almost 2 percent of U.S. electricity, more than New York City and Los Angeles combined, and represented about 0.5 percent of U.S. carbon dioxide emissions. Now, if you think that finding sounds bad, then I hate to break it to you, but the actual emissions picture is probably much, much worse. For one thing, the survey ended in April of last year, and data center development has continued apace since then, with natural gas, and to a somewhat lesser extent, coal, supplying much of the new power demand. Furthermore, as Emily Atkin writes at her great climate newsletter HEATED , the study, for a number of key reasons, “gets nowhere near the actual amount of climate pollution” data centers actually emit. From Atkin’s piece: One [issue] is the way the researchers counted the facilities’ emissions. To do this, they estimated how much electricity each data center used, then looked at how the grid in that part of the country makes its electricity—how much comes from gas, coal, renewables, and so on—to estimate how much CO₂ would be released to generate that much power. But not all data center electricity comes from the grid. Indeed, an ever-increasing number of these massive data centers are also building their own, on-site fossil fuel plants . For example, during the study period (May 2024 through April 2025), Elon Musk’s xAI got some of the electricity for its Colossus data center in Memphis from the grid—but it also got some of it by burning gas in turbines right outside the building. Lead author Gianluca Guidi confirmed that Colossus wasn’t among the 403 facilities studied. TLDR, the study doesn’t count the growing number of data centers, like Colossus, that use gas turbines on-site to power their plants. Furthermore, “electricity consumption is not the only way these facilities heat the planet. For example, the equipment that keeps the servers from overheating is leaking heat-trapping refrigerants into the atmosphere. And when a data center runs on gas—as so many of them do— methane can escape from wells and pipelines before the gas even reaches the power plant. Finally, due to their tracking methodology, the authors may have undercounted the number of data centers in operation at the time the study was carried out by a significant margin. As many as 250 data centers may be absent from the count, as of 2025, Atkin argues. All of which is to say, the study should be viewed as the floor; the minimum for how much greenhouse gas pollution data centers are emitting. And that is more than the entire country of Kenya. The findings of the Harvard study comport rather disconcertingly with those of another recent report, State of AI Climate Impact 2026 , by the Australian climate researcher Ketan Joshi. Joshi’s report concludes that “The AI boom is already worsening greenhouse gas emissions,” and even more concerningly, that it is “potentially emitting more across its lifecycle than all international aviation.” And, surprise, it’s only slated to get worse in coming years if current development patterns hold. This is honestly pretty wild to contemplate here. The AI industry is on track, by some counts—including McKinsey ’s—to generate more emissions than the coal mining industry, or global shipping and aviation. These are two of the most polluting heavy industries in the world, and AI is poised to blow past them. AI is already emitting twice the greenhouse gases of the global aluminum industry, itself a pretty crazy statistic given that aluminum production is a notoriously polluting endeavor. As the report states, “an unchecked continuation of these trends pushes the AI industry into becoming a major global heavy-emitting industry dwarfing both international aviation and international shipping.” Leading the way is the week’s big IPO winner, Anthropic. As I noted up top, Anthropic rose to prominence by burnishing a reputation as the most ethical purveyor of AI. This notably does not extend to environmental or climate concerns, arenas in which the leading AI firm is notably worse than almost all of its competition. Giants like Amazon, Microsoft, and Google may be reneging on their climate pledges, becoming less transparent in their emissions reporting, and diminishing their efforts to power servers and operations with clean energy. Meta, for instance, one of the nation’s largest data center operators, released its latest sustainability report this week, revealing that its emissions rose 45% since last year. The company said it was rethinking its erstwhile climate goals of producing net zero carbon emissions by 2030 as a result. Yet Anthropic hasn’t even bothered to release any information about its carbon emissions or environmental impacts at all. Here’s a rundown from a special section of Joshi’s report focusing just on Anthropic and its posture towards energy and climate issues. It’s pretty damning. I’ll quote from it at length : Anthropic has never disclosed any energy, emissions or environmental data of any kind. In July 2025, Anthropic suggested the US government explicitly set a target for the construction of fossil gas power, promising to begin “preconstruction design work for natural gas plants” by the end of 2026. In May 2026, it was revealed that Anthropic is leasing capacity from the notoriously polluting SpaceX Memphis facility, itself a major source of local air pollution and climate pollution, and a project that has been strongly contested by affected locals; one analyst estimates (based on payments to SpaceX) that 1 in 2 Anthropic queries is served by this fossil-fueled facility (one of the worst in the world). In a recently released set of “data centre community commitments ”, Anthropic promises much of the new power generation to serve their data centres will be “natural gas, which can be brought online quickly, ramps up and down as demand changes, and is abundant in the places we’re considering for data centers”. They claim to be considering renewable energy but do not provide any details, and promise to invest in carbon removal to “help address emissions”. In the S1 form filed by Anthropic, in advance of their Initial Public Offering (IPO), Anthropic suggests long term high emissions by declaring several fossil-fuel related risks, such as exposure to fossil fuel price volatility or competition with other customers for fossil gas. They also dismiss renewables as too high in cost (while ironically stating that “physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time”). In November 2026, Anthropic struck a USD $3.4bn deal with OnePWR, a fossil fuelled turbine manufacturer, for 1.7 gigawatts of generators, with the Financial Times stating that the transaction “is the largest known single purchase of power-generation equipment by an AI lab”. This transaction is more than three times the amount spent by xAI on its notoriously polluting Memphis turbines, and would emit approximately 6 MTCO2-e per year, equivalent to adding 1.8 million fossil-fuelled cars to the road. In November 2026, Anthropic posted a job listing paying up to $405,000 USD per year for “a Gas Supply & Transport Lead to own natural gas supply for Anthropic’s non-cloud data center portfolio in the United States and Canada”, adding that “if gas does not arrive, in the volume and at the pressure the plant needs, the compute does not run”. This is a clear portrait of a company that is not concerned with its own ballooning carbon emissions and climate impacts, until, that is, they threaten to hamper its data centers’ capacity to run smoothly. Image by Janusz Walczak via Unsplash The single biggest threat to AI data centers right now, however, is probably that everyone hates them. They hate them so much that public citizens across the United States have mobilized to shut them down, and elected politicians who’ve promised to help them do so. So how has the AI industry responded? By directing its trade groups and lobby to partner with the fossil fuel industry to push the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, through Congress before the data center-skeptical class of 2027 Democrats arrive. The tech industry is not just buying more fossil fuel power, it’s proactively working to enact policies that make it cheaper, easier and less democratic a process to build more fossil fuel power plants. BAAJA is an assemblage of provisions the fossil fuels industry has been after for years: rollbacks on local governments’ legal tools to curtail development projects, curbs on endangered species protections, and a defanging of the Clean Water Act. Here’s Aaron Rugenberg, an environmental lawyer and the director of Public Citizen’s Climate Accountability Project, explaining in the New Republic : BAAJA severely weakens the Clean Water Act , robbing states and tribes of their ability to protect water quality and require adequate safeguards for activities that pollute or destroy water resources. It practically nullifies the Endangered Species Act by delegating its core responsibilities to the states, most of which either oppose the act’s wildlife protections or lack the expertise and resources to adequately fulfill these obligations. And it essentially repeals the National Environmental Policy Act , the bedrock environmental law that gives the public a voice in decisions that impact the environment, by prohibiting the enforcement of NEPA violations. These three legal frameworks are responsible for most the improvements in water quality, green space, and wildlife recovery in our country over the last half-century. And that’s just the beginning. Other provisions of BAAJA go to even greater lengths to radically lock in fossil fuel development far into the future. The “disparate treatment” section of the bill effectively makes the permitting decisions of the Trump administration permanent. In the words of David Bookbinder , an environmental lawyer who has worked for both the left-leaning Sierra Club and the libertarian Niskanen Center, “The result of making these energy permitting policies permanent is that future administrations will be unable to effectively reduce GHG emissions.” BAAJA also guarantees not just the construction of fossil fuel projects but also their “operation at full capacity,” permanently blocking any future administration from regulating energy infrastructure. And it’s a similar case for data center projects. My friends at the AI Now Institute put out a statement declaring that a vote for BAAJA is “a vote for a ‘backdoor bailout’ of the AI industry.” Why? Two reasons: BAAJA preempts the few levers that local, state, and Tribal authorities have to hold Big Tech accountable. BAAJA supercharges AI data center expansion in exchange for token ratepayer protections. Coming as it is off the heels of the blue wave, anti-AI election, BAAJA feels like a slap in the face to voters. Or as Naomi Klein put it, “The voters just rejected data centers. Why is the Senate trying to fast-track them?” It’s crucial to note that this is not just a Republican/big tech/oil industry-led effort. A bunch of centrist and ‘abundance’ Democrats have joined the GOP in supporting the effort, under the auspices that it will cut red tape for clean energy projects, too. That’s true, to an extent, but this a terrible deal, and an absolutely unnecessary tradeoff at a point when Republicans’ stock could not be lower. After all, a) it’s just as important that we leave fossil fuels in the ground at this late stage of the climate crisis as it is that we build out more clean energy, and b) there are tools to effect desired outcomes without stripping local governments of the power to protect their communities and ecosystems. Regardless, fast-track it the Senate did , with the help of more than a dozen Democratic Senators, including current Majority Leader Chuck Schumer. It now heads to the House of Representatives. I expect this to accelerate calls for a change in Senate leadership. To recap: As of spring in 2025, American data centers were emitting as much greenhouse gas pollution as nations like Kenya, Bolivia, and Denmark. They are almost certainly emitting much more than that today. Worldwide, the AI industry is on a trajectory to outpace the emissions of the heaviest and most-polluting industries, like aviation and coal mining, within the next ten years. And tech firms are fighting to make it easier and faster to build more fossil fuel projects and data centers. In other words, the AI industry is quickly becoming not just a concern, but something more akin to a disaster for the climate. It’s no longer merely prolonging the lifespan of fossil fueled power plants, but actively working to bring more of them online to run their data centers, at a scale that was mostly unthinkable even three years ago. “There’s a kind of dirty ‘energy desperation’ within the industry,” the climate researcher and study author Ketan Joshi tells me. “If you give them 100 wind farms, they’ll take those but still build 5 city-sized gas plants, because the brute force software system they provide has no upper limit on energy consumption.” ”What this means is that regulation that aims to treat the symptoms (eg: 100% renewable mandates, or deregulating permitting to allow for more transmission) just gets added on top of AI consumption,” he adds. “Like fossil fuels in general, we need to limit the source.” There’s one more element to all of this that needs to be underlined, and that’s the fact that the AI industry’s data center and fossil fuel infrastructure buildout won’t just contribute to carbon emissions, but air pollution, too. There’s a real cost to respiratory health, and not just to those who live close to next door to polluting mega-projects like xAI’s Colossus. Dr. Robert Merchant is a pulmonologist in Montana, where a massive 8 square mile data center project has begun construction, built by Quantica Infrastructure, outside of Billings. The project involves bringing online gas-fired power plants to provide 1,800 megawatts of capacity—more capacity than all other power plants currently operating in Montana combined . Merchant submitted a study of the respiratory health impacts a power plant of that size to Yellowstone County, and spoke at a public meeting with the commissioners. Merchant, who I might add is my uncle, and thus perhaps is evidence of a familial predisposition to taking data center interests to task, noted how this level of gas-fired power generation will loose particulate pollution across the state and far beyond. Based on his modeling, the data center project would increase asthma rates, illness rates, as well as the number of heart attacks and strokes. It would cost between $20-50 million in medical costs, dampen productivity in the region as workers take more sick days, and cause 1-2 deaths per year. His report and presentation made news in the local media. Here’s the Montana Free Press : Robert Merchant, a semi-retired Billings Clinic doctor, presented his findings at the commissioners’ Thursday discussion meeting… Fine particles containing nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide, methane and other gases can contribute to asthma, heart attacks, cancer, low birthweight, cognitive functioning and other health problems, he wrote. Merchant said the environmental impacts from the data center, as currently planned, would spill well beyond Yellowstone County, stretching as far south as northern Texas… “Inaction will result in health and economic damage to the public.” Merchant thanked the commissioners for their work and said he hoped the data he shared was useful to their analysis. Merchant’s presentation was met with applause. Get ‘em, uncle Bob. I used my inside connections to reach out to Merchant and ask if there was anything about his report or the situation in Montana he wanted to share with readers. He responded in kind: What frustrates me to no end is that this type of data isn’t part of every single proposal for a new data center. What a complete lack of transparency. Even if they don’t do the modeling of health effects they should be required to state their expected emissions. I had to reach out to acquaintances at an excellent organization, Montana Environmental Information Center, to get the needed estimates. They gathered it up for public, but not easily found, information. A reporter from our local paper had also sourced some of the information. It wasn’t that hard for me to do the analysis and report but why should the region be relying on a retired pulmonologist to figure out the health impacts of this huge new data center? Where is the EPA? Where is the Montana Department of Environmental Quality? Where is the Yellowstone County Public Health Department? Or even more idealistically, shouldn’t the company itself care about the region and do the analysis themselves? And share it with the community? I could not agree more. Speaking of, this kind of transparency would be some very low-hanging fruit that the new wave of data center-critical politicians could demand when they take office. The AI industry and its data center buildout are on track to become a genuine crisis factor for the climate, especially given its limitless appetite for expansion. And it’s funny, you never hear the AI execs promise that their products are going to “solve” climate change anymore. Now they stick to saying it will cure cancer. Saying AI is good for climate now apparently creates too much cognitive dissonance for the tech elite to stomach, and that’s saying something. Subscribe Some fun media stuff this week: I joined KQED’s Forum with Washington Post tech reporter Shira Ovide and former Biden AI policy advisor Ben Buchanan. We talked Nvidia, Anthropic, the global internet outages, and more. It’s always a good time joining Alexis’s show. I was interviewed for the BBC’s Global Story, for an episode about AI and Luddites, which was particularly cool. It’s n+1 Bookmatch season , which longtime readers know is one of my favorite holiday traditions. If you haven’t taken it yet, get to it; donate to a great literary mag and find some stellar reads in the process. I got at least one home run already, which I somehow missed until now: Matthew Wolfe’s Fires in the Night, a history of the Earth Liberation Front, a group with some strong Luddite vibes indeed. Finally, if you didn’t catch it, for the show this week I sat down with Cory Doctorow to talk about how AI is breaking the internet. This is already one of our biggest shows on YouTube, for perhaps the obvious reasons. No one does this better than Cory. Alright, that’s it for now. As always, thanks for reading. content.full_text: AI people are very, very, very, very rich What should we think about that? Noah Smith Nov 22, 2026 ∙ Paid 294 120 38 As you may have heard, Anthropic had its IPO this past Thursday. At a valuation of $1.5 trillion, it was actually just the second most valuable IPO in history, just behind SpaceX at $1.77 trillion. I bought some shares on the first day at what I thought was a reasonable price, only to see my shares drop the following day as the company’s valuation fell to $1.175 trillion, making it only the 14th most valuable company in the world. Such are the risks of buying individual stocks! But that price drop doesn’t change the fact that Anthropic’s IPO was a staggeringly large wealth creation event. Anthropic began hiring lots of employees just a few years ago; now, almost all of those people have either hundreds of millions of dollars, or tens of millions of dollars. Andrew Benson had a good breakdown of exactly who would get what, if the company hit its initial valuation target of $2 trillion: Who actually gets rich if Anthropic lists at $2 trillion?… - $199B for the 7 controlling co-founders, about 10% - $28B for Ben Mann, if his stake matches theirs - $100B for the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, 5% - $331B in employee options and RSUs, about 17% , That pool covers about 5,300 employees, an average of $62M each… [H]ere is roughly how many people made what at $2T: - $110M to $400M each: ~300 to 500 people hired by 2023 - $200M to $300M each: ~440 to 640 hired in 2024 - $70M to $95M each: ~1,360 hired in 2025 - $10M to $20M each: ~3,000 hired in 2026 So about 940 people hired by the end of 2024 average nine figures. Everyone hired since averages eight figures. The company’s (fully diluted) valuation is now only about 80% of that $2T number, so you have to scale those numbers down a little bit. But it’s still a staggering amount of money for just a few years of work! We’re used to seeing the first few employees at a generational company make hundreds of millions of dollars, but seeing several hundred people make that much is just unprecedented. Let’s put these numbers in perspective. If Anthropic were worth $2T, it would have more centimillionaires than the entire city of Los Angeles. Even with only 350-400 centimillionaires, that’s about as many as Houston, Dallas, and Austin combined: Steve Rattner @ SteveRattner There are now more hundred millionaires at Anthropic than in all of Los Angeles. 3:16 PM · Nov 20, 2026 · 101K Views 52 Replies · 269 Reposts · 1.84K Likes By some reckonings, Anthropic now has between 0.5% and 1.3% of all the centimillionaires in the U.S. Collectively, the company’s founders and employees have as much wealth as the entire bottom third of Americans, combined: Source: Steve Rattner Of course, just looking at these numbers tremendously understates the amount of wealth that has been created in the AI industry over the last couple of years. There’s also OpenAI, which is targeting an IPO valuation of $1.25 trillion. And there are quite a number of AI startups that have gotten very valuable, very quickly. Just a few include Isomorphic Labs at ~$50 billion, Cognition at $48 billion, Prometheus at $41 billion, Safe Superintelligence at $32 billion, VAST Data at $30 billion, Reflection AI at ~$27.5 billion, Cohere at $25.5 billion, ElevenLabs at $22 billion, and so on. And of course, all of this is just today . I wouldn’t have bought Anthropic stock unless I thought the company had a very good chance of becoming much more valuable than it is today. Despite the early price drop, I’m still very bullish. I think AI’s extremely cross-domain capabilities mean that Anthropic has a good shot at being a very large, diversified conglomerate: Anthropic’s moat is Claude Noah Smith · Nov 2 Read full story Furthermore, I think the company is amassing a huge pool of top human talent, essentially giving them a hedge against a future in which AI continues to be a complement to top human talent rather than a substitute. Almost every smart person I know here in Silicon Valley either works there or has strongly considered working there. That makes Anthropic resemble Google back in 2004, which became a legendary brain trust. If anyone can figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI, it’s probably Anthropic. And yes, someone will figure out a way to make boatloads of money with AI. Even if that means the company only becomes as valuable as Google or Microsoft is today , that means I’ll more than double my own investment. If that happens, all of those wealth numbers from the top of this post will also more than double. And if the U.S. economy grows robustly and AI itself grows rapidly as a percentage of that economy, this could easily turn out to be the greatest wealth creation event in American history, by far — greater than the internet, far greater than crypto, greater even than the railroads. I can definitely feel this wealth all around me. A lot of the people I went to potlucks with three years ago now have an order of magnitude more money than anyone I ever met before I turned 30. Some of those people are under 30 themselves. A few of them are billionaires. Now, when I go to house parties, they’re often in lavish designer-furnished mansions overlooking spectacular ocean views from high up on San Francisco hilltops. As a social phenomenon, this is totally unprecedented. Sarah Chieng writes : You can build a startup in 9 months, get acquired (but rly acquihired) by OpenAI, Anthropic, or Cognition, and walk away a multi-millionaire…You can join the right company at 22 and become effectively post-economic…And I don't think we've even begun to grapple with the degree to which this is warping an entire generation's relationship with money, ambition, work, and success…When your peers are making generational wealth before 25, what does a normal career even look like anymore[?] I’m happy for my friends, of course. And I am not personally bothered by seeing displays of great wealth. But I find myself wondering what this is going to do to my society. If the AI class are the only people who get rich going forward, what kind of tensions will that produce among the country’s elites? What would it mean for America if wealth inequality goes up far further even than it already has? What if only the AI people get rich?
